These results suggested that recipient-dependent extrinsic factors, rather than intrinsic factors of transplanted HSCs, had a greater impact on hematopoietic cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from transplantation experiments showing that the same young LT-HSCs produce different lineage outputs depending on recipient age.

claims.claim: Cell interaction with niche cells in bone marrow is altered with age.
claims.source: Multiple extrinsic factors have been implicated as HSC-independent causes of myeloid-biased hematopoiesis associated with aging. Some findings suggest that cell interaction with niche cells in BM is altered (Pinho et al., 2018), whereas others claim that chronic inflammation in aged mice lowers production of lymphoid progenitors and induces myeloid-biased hematopoiesis (Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Ergen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from Pinho et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Chronic inflammation in aged mice lowers production of lymphoid progenitors and induces myeloid-biased hematopoiesis.
claims.source: Multiple extrinsic factors have been implicated as HSC-independent causes of myeloid-biased hematopoiesis associated with aging. Some findings suggest that cell interaction with niche cells in BM is altered (Pinho et al., 2018), whereas others claim that chronic inflammation in aged mice lowers production of lymphoid progenitors and induces myeloid-biased hematopoiesis (Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Ergen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019 and Ergen et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to a relative decrease in the ratio of mature lymphocytes in peripheral blood, resulting from inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the bone marrow.
claims.source: These findings suggest that myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to a relative decrease in the ratio of mature lymphocytes in PB, resulting from inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the BM, such as in the thymus and spleen, rather than a significant change in cell differentiation caused by the intramedullary environment.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations showing normal bone marrow progenitors but reduced lymphocytes in aged spleens and thymi.

claims.claim: Administering keratinocyte growth factor restores lymphocyte hematopoiesis in aged mice.
claims.source: Attempts have been made in the past to restore thymus function in aged mice by administering keratinocyte growth factor (Rossi et al., 2007b). Indeed, in aged mice, lymphocyte hematopoiesis recovers, which is consistent with our results that the extramedullary environment influences the myeloid-bias phenotype in PB (Rossi et al., 2007b).
claims.evidence: Cited from Rossi et al., 2007b.

claims.claim: Recovery of the lymphocyte fraction in peripheral blood is delayed in elderly donors compared to young donors.
claims.source: It has been clinically documented that recovery of the lymphocyte fraction in PB is delayed in elderly donors, compared to young donors (González-Vicent et al., 2017; Baron et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Cited from González-Vicent et al., 2017 and Baron et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Lymphocyte recovery is delayed in elderly patients compared to younger patients.
claims.source: It has also been noted that lymphocyte recovery is delayed in elderly patients compared to younger patients (Berger et al., 2008; van der Maas et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Cited from Berger et al., 2008 and van der Maas et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Age-related loss in thymus and spleen functions has been recorded in humans.
claims.source: Age-related loss in thymus and spleen functions has been recorded in humans, implying that the same mechanism is acting as in our mouse observations.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge about human aging.

claims.claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice originates due to alteration of the ratio between LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs rather than in heterogeneous HSC clones with various cell fates.
claims.source: Thus, we demonstrate that myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice originates due to alteration of the ratio between LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs rather than in heterogeneous HSC clones with various cell fates.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experiments showing that manipulating LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratios recapitulates age-related myeloid bias.

claims.claim: While the niche environment in the bone marrow minimally affects myeloid-biased hematopoiesis, aged thymi and spleens substantially hinder lymphoid hematopoiesis, resulting in further myeloid domination.
claims.source: In addition, while the niche environment in the bone marrow minimally affects myeloid-biased hematopoiesis, aged thymi and spleens substantially hinder lymphoid hematopoiesis, resulting in further myeloid domination.
claims.evidence: Supported by experiments showing normal bone marrow progenitors but impaired lymphoid development in aged secondary lymphoid organs.

claims.claim: Young and aged LT-HSCs co-transplanted into the same recipients demonstrated nearly equivalent myeloid lineage output.
claims.source: Utilizing the Hoxb5 reporter system to prospectively isolate long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs) and short-term HSCs (ST-HSCs), we found that young and aged LT-HSCs co-transplanted into the same recipients demonstrated nearly equivalent myeloid lineage output, contrary to the theory of myeloid-biased HSC clones.
claims.evidence: Supported by co-transplantation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Transcriptomics indicated no significant myeloid gene enrichment in aged LT-HSCs compared to their young counterparts.
claims.source: Transcriptomics indicated no significant myeloid gene enrichment in aged LT-HSCs compared to their young counterparts.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis and GSEA shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Transplanting reconstituted young HSCs with the ratio of LT/ST-HSCs seen in aged mice can significantly skew the lineage output to myeloid cells.
claims.source: Instead, transplanting reconstituted young HSCs with the ratio of LT/ST-HSCs seen in aged mice can significantly skew the lineage output to myeloid cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6.

results.result: Age-associated changes in peripheral blood myeloid cells do not correlate with changes in bone marrow HSC and progenitor populations. While myeloid cells in peripheral blood increase steadily from 6 months onward, HSC frequency increases rapidly until 12 months then slows, GMP remains stable, and CMP actually decreases with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by longitudinal flow cytometry data across multiple age groups (Figure 1A-C). The discordance between peripheral blood and bone marrow compartments challenges the prevailing hypothesis that myeloid-biased HSC clones drive age-related myeloid bias, providing a key observation that motivates the rest of the study.

results.result: Hoxb5 specifically marks LT-HSCs in aged mice, as demonstrated by exclusive expression in bulk-HSCs and robust long-term reconstitution capacity in primary and secondary transplantation assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 2A) and serial transplantation data (Figure 2C-F). The validation of Hoxb5 as an LT-HSC marker in aged mice is critical for the study's methodology, as it enables prospective isolation of functionally defined HSC subsets rather than relying on surface markers alone.

results.result: The myeloid output kinetics of aged LT-HSCs remain consistent across primary and secondary transplantation.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is supported by data in Figure 2G showing similar myeloid proportions across serial transplants. However, this observation alone is insufficient to rule out myeloid-biased clonal expansion, as the authors acknowledge that myeloid bias may have already peaked by 2 years of age.

results.result: Young and aged LT-HSCs exhibit equivalent differentiation potential when co-transplanted into the same recipients, with comparable myeloid and lymphoid lineage output throughout the observation period.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C70 are based on co-transplantation data (Figure 3B-D) showing similar lineage output between young and aged LT-HSCs. However, the authors acknowledge the small sample size (n=8) and note that subtle differences cannot be entirely ruled out. The myeloid output was 51.4±31.5% for young vs 47.4±39.0% for aged LT-HSCs (p=0.82), but the large standard deviations and modest sample size limit confidence in detecting small but potentially meaningful differences.

results.result: Aged bulk-HSCs exhibit myeloid-skewed hematopoiesis compared to young bulk-HSCs in competitive transplantation assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by co-transplantation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D). This result confirms previous literature findings and establishes an important contrast with the LT-HSC results, suggesting that the myeloid bias resides in the bulk-HSC population composition rather than in LT-HSCs themselves.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis reveals no significant myeloid or lymphoid gene set enrichment in aged LT-HSCs or ST-HSCs, while aged bulk-HSCs show a non-significant trend toward myeloid gene enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 and C71 are supported by RNA-seq and GSEA data (Figure 4F-G). The authors appropriately address the reproducibility issues in HSC aging transcriptomics by using only genes shared across multiple published gene sets. The lack of significant myeloid enrichment in aged LT-HSCs supports the conclusion that myeloid bias is not due to cell-intrinsic transcriptional changes in LT-HSCs.

results.result: The apparent lymphoid bias observed after ST-HSC transplantation is due to persistence of memory T cells in peripheral blood rather than ongoing lymphopoiesis, as ST-HSC recipients lack HSCs in bone marrow and their lymphocytes are predominantly memory phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by transplantation kinetics (Figure 5B), T cell phenotyping (Figure 5C-D), and bone marrow analysis (Figure 5E-F). This is a critical mechanistic insight that reinterprets previous observations of 'lymphoid-biased' HSCs, showing they reflect cell longevity rather than differentiation bias.

results.result: The ratio of ST-HSCs to LT-HSCs within the bulk-HSC compartment decreases with age.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing age-dependent changes in LT-HSC and ST-HSC frequencies. This observation is central to the study's main hypothesis that altered HSC subset ratios, rather than clonal selection, drive myeloid-biased hematopoiesis.

results.result: Reconstituting young HSCs with an aged LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio (5:5) recapitulates myeloid-biased hematopoiesis, with significantly higher myeloid output by 16 weeks compared to a young ratio (2:8).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 and C72 are supported by transplantation data (Figure 6B-D) showing time-dependent emergence of myeloid bias in the 5:5 ratio group. This is a key experiment demonstrating that altering the LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio is sufficient to produce myeloid bias without requiring myeloid-biased clones, directly testing the study's central hypothesis.

results.result: Transplanting aged HSCs at a 2:8 LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio (mimicking young mice) produces significantly more lymphoid output than a 5:5 ratio (mimicking aged mice).
results.evaluation: Claim C25 is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D. This reciprocal experiment strengthens the conclusion that the LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio is a key determinant of lineage output, showing the effect is bidirectional and not specific to young cells.

results.result: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice is caused by a relative decrease in ST-HSCs within the bulk-HSC compartment rather than selective expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones.
results.evaluation: Claims C26 and C68 represent the study's main conclusion, supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: equivalent differentiation of young vs aged LT-HSCs (C11-C13), lack of myeloid gene enrichment in aged LT-HSCs (C16-C17), decreased ST-HSC ratio with age (C22), and recapitulation of myeloid bias by manipulating LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratios (C23-C25). The logic is sound and the experimental support is substantial.

results.result: Young LT-HSCs transplanted into aged recipients produce significantly more myeloid cells than when transplanted into young recipients, indicating that recipient age influences lineage output.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C60 are supported by peripheral blood analysis (Figure 7C-E) comparing young vs aged recipients. This demonstrates that extrinsic, recipient-dependent factors contribute to myeloid bias beyond the intrinsic HSC changes, adding an important layer to the mechanistic understanding.

results.result: Bone marrow progenitor frequencies (CMP, GMP, CLP) are similar between young and aged recipients of young LT-HSCs, suggesting that intramedullary age-associated changes do not significantly impact LT-HSC differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by bone marrow analysis (Figure 7F). However, the sample size is limited (n=8 per group, selected from survivors), and the conclusion contradicts some prior studies (Pinho et al., 2018; Ergen et al., 2012). The authors appropriately note this discrepancy but do not fully address potential methodological differences.

results.result: Donor cell frequencies in spleens and thymi are significantly reduced in aged compared to young recipients of young LT-HSCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 7G, I) and flow cytometry (Figure 7H, J). This identifies extramedullary lymphoid organ dysfunction as a contributor to myeloid-biased peripheral blood composition in aged mice.

results.result: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice results from impaired lymphocyte maturation in aged thymus and spleen rather than changes in bone marrow differentiation, with the bone marrow niche having minimal impact while aged secondary lymphoid organs substantially hinder lymphopoiesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C63 and C69 synthesize findings from bone marrow (C28-C29) and secondary lymphoid organ analyses (C31-C32). The conclusion is well-supported by the data showing normal bone marrow progenitors but reduced lymphoid output in aged secondary organs. This represents an important mechanistic insight into the extrinsic contribution to age-related myeloid bias.

results.result: The degree of myeloid bias in naturally aged mice (≥23 months) is significantly greater than in young recipients receiving reconstituted HSCs with an aged LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by comparison of Figure 1A (49.0±23.4% myeloid in aged mice) and Figure 6D (30.8±30.8% myeloid in 5:5 ratio recipients). This observation indicates that altered LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratios alone cannot fully explain the myeloid bias in naturally aged mice, motivating the investigation of additional extrinsic factors.

results.result: Background and literature context establishing the prevailing hypotheses about age-related myeloid-biased hematopoiesis, HSC biology, and prior experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C67 represent cited background knowledge and prior work. These are appropriately referenced and provide necessary context for the study. The authors accurately represent the field's understanding and controversies, though the accuracy of individual citations would require verification of the original sources.

results.result: The authors characterize age-associated changes in hematopoietic cell populations, showing that myeloid cells in peripheral blood increase progressively with age (C1), HSC frequency increases rapidly until 12 months then slows (C2), while GMP frequency remains stable (C3) and CMP frequency decreases (C4), with these bone marrow changes not paralleling peripheral blood myeloid increases (C5).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that the assumption linking CMP/GMP changes to myeloid-biased HSC expansion is 'misleading' and that 'the link between these two changes could be more complex than just a direct correlation.' This critique suggests the interpretation of these progenitor data in relation to the myeloid bias phenotype is oversimplified and not fully supported.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that Hoxb5 is exclusively expressed in bulk-HSCs in aged mice (C6) and that only Hoxb5+ HSCs maintain long-term reconstitution in primary (C7) and secondary (C8) transplantation, establishing Hoxb5 as a specific marker of LT-HSCs in both young and aged mice (C9).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises fundamental concerns about sample size and representativeness, noting that '10 out of so many old HSCs (an average of 300,000 up to 500,000 cells per mouse)' may not 'faithfully represent old HSC population.' The reviewer calculates that the total cells used represent only '3.2 mice experiment for the whole manuscript,' which is 'not enough, especially for old mice experiments considering the heterogeneity of aged mice.' Reviewer 2 also notes 'very low number of recipient mice, showed very large standard deviations' weakening the conclusions.

results.result: The kinetics of myeloid cell proportions in peripheral blood were similar across primary and secondary transplantation of aged LT-HSCs.
results.evaluation: This descriptive finding about transplantation kinetics is not directly challenged by reviewers, though it is part of experiments with broader methodological concerns about sample size and variability.

results.result: Co-transplantation experiments show that young and aged LT-HSCs produce nearly comparable myeloid lineage output (C11, C70), with similar reconstitution ratios across all lineages (C12), leading to the conclusion that LT-HSC differentiation potential remains unchanged throughout life (C13).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 directly challenges this key finding: 'Given the large standard deviation and low n-numbers, the power of the analysis to detect differences between experimental groups is very low... The absence of clearly detectable differences between young and aged transplanted HSCs could thus simply be a false-negative result.' Reviewer 1 echoes this concern about representativeness. Reviewer 3 notes 'the level of variability in key in vivo experiments (Figure 2 and 3) diminishes the robustness of these results' and that 'a more rigorous statistical analysis should be performed.' These are central claims attempting to overturn the field's paradigm, but reviewers find the evidence insufficient.

results.result: Aged bulk-HSCs exhibited a myeloid-skewed phenotype compared to young bulk-HSCs in transplantation assays.
results.evaluation: This observation of myeloid bias in bulk-HSCs is consistent with prior literature and not challenged by reviewers. It serves as a control showing the expected phenotype in mixed HSC populations.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis shows that neither aged LT-HSCs nor aged ST-HSCs exhibited significant myeloid or lymphoid gene set enrichment (C16, C71), while aged bulk-HSCs showed only a non-significant trend toward myeloid gene enrichment (C17).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identifies a logical inconsistency: 'since ST-HSCs do not exhibit lymphoid gene set enrichment based on their data, it is hard to understand how aged bulk HSCs have more myeloid gene set enrichment compared to young bulk HSCs. This bulk HSC data rather suggest that there could be a trend toward certain lineage bias (although not significant) in aged LT-HSCs or ST-HSCs.' The reviewer requests verification 'using another comprehensive dataset.' This critique suggests the molecular data do not definitively rule out lineage bias in LT-HSCs.

results.result: ST-HSC recipients show lymphocyte-dominant hematopoiesis over time (C18) with predominantly memory T cells (C19) and no bulk-HSCs in bone marrow (C20), suggesting this lymphoid bias results from persistent memory lymphocytes rather than ongoing lymphopoiesis (C21).
results.evaluation: These observations about ST-HSC behavior and the interpretation regarding memory cell persistence are not directly challenged by reviewers. The data appear internally consistent for this specific finding.

results.result: The ratio of ST-HSC to LT-HSC decreases with age in the bulk-HSC population.
results.evaluation: This descriptive observation about changing HSC subset ratios with age is not challenged by reviewers and forms the basis for the authors' alternative model.

results.result: Manipulating the LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio in transplantation experiments shows that a 5:5 ratio produces more myeloid-biased hematopoiesis than a 2:8 ratio (C23, C24), with reciprocal effects on lymphoid output (C25), leading to the conclusion that altered LT/ST ratios rather than myeloid-biased clones cause age-related myeloid bias (C26, C72).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 questions the logic: 'It is not intuitively clear why a reduction of ST-HSCs clones would lead to a myeloid bias. The author should try to explain more clearly where they believe the increased number of myeloid cells comes from.' Reviewer 1 questions whether the cell numbers used 'represent old HSC (either LT or ST) behavior' and notes that 'old ST-HSC functional data showed that they barely contribute to blood production unlike young Hoxb5- HSCs.' The biological significance of Figure S6.D is questioned as 'questionable how biologically meaningful it is.' These concerns suggest the mechanism proposed is not convincingly demonstrated.

results.result: Young LT-HSCs transplanted into aged recipients produce more myeloid cells than in young recipients (C27, C60), while bone marrow progenitor frequencies (CMP, GMP, CLP) remain similar between young and aged recipients (C28, C29), suggesting intramedullary age-associated changes have minimal impact on LT-HSC differentiation (C30).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'did not address the comment regarding inflammatory aged niche effects,' which was a key concern about extrinsic factors. Reviewer 3 points out that 'the chosen irradiation regiment might contribute to the uncertainty of the data' with 'concerningly high' radioresistant cells in secondary transplants, making it 'difficult to compare those studies with the present manuscript.' These methodological issues undermine confidence in the conclusions about niche effects.

results.result: Aged recipients show significantly reduced donor cell frequencies in thymus and spleen compared to young recipients (C31, C32), leading to the conclusion that myeloid bias results from impaired lymphocyte maturation in aged extramedullary organs rather than altered HSC differentiation (C63, C69).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'Their data regarding the role of the microenvironment in the spleen and thymus appears to be convincing.' This aspect of the work receives positive evaluation despite concerns about other findings.

results.result: The degree of myeloid bias in naturally aged mice (≥23 months) is significantly greater than in recipients of young mixed HSCs at a 5:5 LT:ST ratio 16 weeks post-transplantation.
results.evaluation: This comparative observation is not directly challenged and suggests additional factors beyond LT/ST ratio contribute to the full aged phenotype.

results.result: The authors' main conclusion that myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice originates from altered LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratios rather than expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'the current results remain incomplete and additional data are necessary to substantiate the conclusions.' Reviewer 2 concludes 'the presented data remain weak and do not convincingly challenge the current paradigm' and that 'the overall conclusions of this manuscript thus remain weak and preliminary.' Reviewer 1 states 'this study needs more definitive data.' Reviewer 3 notes 'such a strong claim needs to be supported by solid experimental data' but 'the level of variability in key in vivo experiments (Figure 2 and 3) diminishes the robustness of these results.' All reviewers find the central claim insufficiently supported.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims C1-C5 about peripheral blood and bone marrow progenitor changes with age. OpenEval finds these claims well-supported by flow cytometry data, while peer reviewers (Reviewer 3) find the interpretation UNCERTAIN, noting the link between CMP/GMP changes and myeloid-biased HSC expansion is 'misleading' and 'more complex than just a direct correlation.'

Both evaluate claims C6-C9 regarding Hoxb5 as an LT-HSC marker validation. OpenEval finds the validation SUPPORTED by flow cytometry and transplantation data. Peer reviewers find this UNCERTAIN due to fundamental concerns about sample size and representativeness, with Reviewer 1 noting only '3.2 mice experiment for the whole manuscript' and Reviewer 2 citing 'very low number of recipient mice' with 'very large standard deviations.'

Both evaluate claim C10 about similar myeloid proportions across serial transplants. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED but notes it alone is insufficient to rule out myeloid-biased clonal expansion. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED as a descriptive finding, though they note broader methodological concerns about the experiments containing this observation.

Both evaluate claims C11-C13, C70 about similar lineage output between young and aged LT-HSCs. OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN due to small sample size (n=8) and large standard deviations. Peer reviewers rate this UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 stating the 'absence of clearly detectable differences...could simply be a false-negative result' and Reviewer 3 noting 'the level of variability...diminishes the robustness of these results.' This is a critical disagreement on a paradigm-challenging claim.

Both evaluate claims C14-C15 about myeloid bias in bulk-HSCs. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find this SUPPORTED, noting it is consistent with prior literature and serves as an important control showing expected phenotype in mixed HSC populations.

Both evaluate claims C16-C17, C71 about lack of myeloid gene enrichment in aged LT-HSCs. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by RNA-seq and GSEA data. Peer reviewers find this UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 identifying a logical inconsistency: if ST-HSCs lack lymphoid enrichment, 'it is hard to understand how aged bulk HSCs have more myeloid gene set enrichment,' suggesting the molecular data do not definitively rule out lineage bias in LT-HSCs.

Both evaluate claims C18-C21 about ST-HSC behavior and memory cell persistence. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find this SUPPORTED. The data appear internally consistent and this interpretation is not challenged by reviewers.

Both evaluate claim C22 about age-dependent changes in LT-HSC and ST-HSC frequencies. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find this SUPPORTED as a descriptive observation that forms the basis for the authors' alternative model.

Both evaluate claims about LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio manipulation experiments. OpenEval (R9: C23-C24, C72) finds this SUPPORTED as a key experiment demonstrating the ratio effect. Peer reviewers (R9: C23-C25, C26, C72) find this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 questioning the logic ('not intuitively clear why a reduction of ST-HSCs clones would lead to a myeloid bias') and Reviewer 1 questioning whether the cell numbers represent actual old HSC behavior.

OpenEval R10 evaluates claim C25 (reciprocal experiment with aged cells) and finds it SUPPORTED. This overlaps with peer R9 which includes C25 among claims rated UNCERTAIN due to concerns about biological meaningfulness and whether the experiments truly represent old HSC behavior.

Both evaluate the study's main conclusion (C26, C68) that myeloid bias results from altered HSC subset ratios rather than clonal selection. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by convergence of multiple lines of evidence. Peer reviewers find this UNSUPPORTED, with the editor stating 'current results remain incomplete,' Reviewer 2 concluding the data 'do not convincingly challenge the current paradigm,' and Reviewer 3 noting 'such a strong claim needs to be supported by solid experimental data.'

OpenEval R12 evaluates claims C27, C60 about recipient age effects on myeloid bias and finds them SUPPORTED. Peer R10 evaluates overlapping claims C27-C30, C60 about extrinsic niche effects and finds them UNCERTAIN, noting the authors 'did not address the comment regarding inflammatory aged niche effects' and that the irradiation regimen 'might contribute to the uncertainty of the data.'

OpenEval R13 evaluates claims C28-C30 about bone marrow progenitor composition and finds them SUPPORTED despite limited sample size. Peer R10 includes these claims in their UNCERTAIN evaluation, citing unaddressed concerns about inflammatory niche effects and methodological issues with the irradiation regiment.

OpenEval R14 evaluates claims C31-C32 about secondary lymphoid organ dysfunction and finds them SUPPORTED by imaging and flow cytometry. Peer R11 evaluates the same claims (plus C63, C69) and finds them SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 specifically noting 'Their data regarding the role of the microenvironment in the spleen and thymus appears to be convincing.'

OpenEval R15 evaluates claims C63, C69 synthesizing findings about extrinsic contributions and finds them SUPPORTED. Peer R11 evaluates these claims (along with C31-C32) and also finds them SUPPORTED, representing one of the few areas of strong agreement between OpenEval and peer reviewers.

Both evaluate claim C59 about the observation that altered LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratios alone cannot fully explain myeloid bias in naturally aged mice. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find this SUPPORTED as a comparative observation indicating additional factors contribute to the aged phenotype.

OpenEval R17 evaluates claims C35-C67 representing cited background knowledge and prior work, finding them appropriately referenced and SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these background claims specifically.
